slide.title: One Token at a Time
slide.body: A row of rounded token blocks: 'The' 'capital' 'of' 'France' 'is' and a glowing empty block with a question mark. Small tag: Generative AI Explained · Lesson 2.

scenes.on_screen_text: From one guess to a page
scenes.voiceover: When you type see you on your phone, the keyboard suggests tomorrow, or soon. A large language model does something very similar, but it can write a full report this way. How does a simple guess about the next word become a whole page?
In the last lesson, we placed language models on our map. Now let's look inside. A language model does not read text the way you do. First, it splits the text into small pieces called tokens.

slide.title: What is a token?
slide.body: 'cat' → one block. 'unbelievable' → three blocks: 'un' | 'believ' | 'able'. '2026' and '!' as blocks. Arrow: each block → a row of numbers.

scenes.voiceover: A token can be a short word, like cat. It can be part of a longer word. Unbelievable might become three pieces. It can also be a number or a punctuation mark. Each token is turned into numbers the model can work with.

slide.title: Different tools, different tokens
slide.body: Same sentence split two ways: Tool A shows 9 blocks, Tool B shows 11 blocks.

scenes.voiceover: Different models split text in different ways. So the same sentence can have a different number of tokens in different tools.

slide.title: Next-token prediction
slide.body: 'The capital of France is' → bar chart of candidate next tokens: Paris (very tall), Lyon (short), a (short), located (short).

scenes.voiceover: Then the model does one job, again and again. It looks at all the tokens so far, and it calculates how likely each possible next token is. After the capital of France is, the token Paris gets a very high score.

slide.title: Repeat, one token at a time
slide.body: Loop diagram: Look at all tokens → Score next token → Choose one → Add it → back to start. Text grows by one block each turn.

scenes.voiceover: The model chooses a token, adds it to the text, and repeats the process with the new, longer text. One token at a time, it builds sentences, paragraphs and pages.

slide.title: Two important facts
slide.body: 1. Likely text, not checked facts. 2. The whole conversation counts, not only the last word.

scenes.voiceover: This explains two important facts. The model writes by choosing likely text, not by looking up checked facts. And it looks at the whole conversation each time, not only the last word. That is why it can keep the same topic and style.

scenes.stock_query: person typing message on smartphone close up
scenes.voiceover: So it is like the suggestions on your phone keyboard, but trained on far more text. Now, the model does not always pick the most likely token. A setting called temperature controls how much variety it allows.

slide.title: Low vs high temperature
slide.body: Left, Low: always tap the first suggestion; predictable; good for summaries and data. Right, High: sometimes tap the second or third; varied, creative; can drift off topic.

scenes.voiceover: At a low temperature, it picks the most likely tokens almost every time. Answers are predictable, which suits summaries or extracting data. At a high temperature, less likely tokens get more chance. Answers are more varied and creative, but they can drift off topic. Think of always tapping the first suggestion, or sometimes the second or third.
Let's try it. Tomasz leads a customer support team at an online furniture shop in Kraków. He wants a model to write short replies to customers, so he tests one prompt in Google AI Studio.

screen_steps: Open Google AI Studio in a browser and sign in with a Google account
Start a new chat or prompt
Point to the run settings panel and highlight the Temperature control
scenes.voiceover: He opens Google AI Studio in his browser, signs in with a Google account and starts a new prompt. On the right is the run settings panel, with the temperature control.

screen_steps: Drag the Temperature slider near the bottom of the range
Paste the prompt: 'Write a two-sentence reply to a customer whose sofa delivery is one day late.'
Run the prompt and copy the answer into a notes file
Run the same prompt two more times and copy both answers
scenes.voiceover: He sets the temperature low, near the bottom of the range. Then he pastes his prompt. Write a two-sentence reply to a customer whose sofa delivery is one day late. He runs it three times and copies each answer.

screen_steps: Show the three low-temperature answers side by side in the notes file
Drag the Temperature slider near the top of the range
Run the same prompt three more times and copy each answer
scenes.voiceover: The three replies are almost the same. A polite apology, and a new delivery date. Now he moves the temperature near the top of the range and runs the same prompt three more times.

screen_steps: Show the three high-temperature answers side by side
Highlight the discount code, the informal tone and the 'free cushion' promise
Type a note: 'Customer replies: low temperature'
scenes.voiceover: This time the replies differ more. One offers a discount code. One uses a very informal tone. And one promises a free cushion, which the shop does not offer. Tomasz decides that customer replies need a low temperature. The shop cannot promise things it does not provide.

scenes.on_screen_text: Fluent text is not checked text.
scenes.voiceover: A common mistake is to think the model knows the full answer first and then types it out. It does not. It predicts each token from what came before. So a small change can send the answer in a new direction. Fluent text is likely text, not checked text.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Tokens in, next token out, again and again. 2. Likely text ≠ correct text. 3. Temperature: low = predictable, high = varied.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, a language model splits text into tokens and writes by predicting the next token, again and again. Second, it chooses likely text based on the whole conversation, so fluent answers are not automatically correct. Third, temperature controls variety. Low values are more predictable, and high values are more varied.

scenes.on_screen_text: Next: How a Language Model Is Trained
scenes.voiceover: Now you try. In the exercise below, run one prompt three times at a low temperature and three times at a high temperature in Google AI Studio. Then describe the difference in two sentences. It takes about twenty minutes. Next, we look at how a language model is trained. See you there.
